As was seen in the ampus area, without benefit of controls, these few modern structures do not fit well into the original design fabric. However, in summary in isolated areas where traffic is less frequent (especially west of Seventeenth Street), the original design integrity still prevails. One distinctive drawback to the original design is the seemingly unnecessarily generous street widths; the area's wide streets contribute to a lack of cohesion which Olinder, for example, possesses.
At the approximate center of the northside neighborhood is located the block-square Backesto Park. While from a design point-of-view its connection to the neighborhood is not as strong as it could be, in terms of possession it undoubtedly belongs to Northside residents. As can be observed on any summer week-end, the park has an important social as well as recreational function in the life of the neighborhood.
Interesting land use effects of major transportation corridors occur in the north-western and northeastern corners of the project area. Whereas northside is predominantly residential, along the southern pacific railroad tracks, industrial land uses are located. This is an older industrial area, and is not without visual interest. However a better integration between it and the surrounding residences seems warranted.
The Bayshore Freeway cuts through the northeast portion of the project area. The irregular parcels created by the freeway are now occupied by modern constructions, including Watson Park, a recently-completed housing tract, apartment buildings, and a trailer park.
Olinder CNRA:
A neighborhood of approximately the same age as Campus is Olinder. Olinder is also similar to Campus in that it is organized on a street grid pattern, and its boundaries are well-drawn to create an enclosed atmosphere.
Olinder is primarily residential; only along its boundaries are there located some commercial uses (along Santa Clara and E. Twenty-Fourth Streets) and industrial activities (centered at William Street and the railroad tracks).
In many respects Olinder resembles the "picture-book" suburban landscape of 20-30 years and the grid are generally adorned with street trees; lot sizes and setbacks are more or less uniform. The housing comes in many architectural styles; however the fact that dissimilar styles stand side by side is softened by the street landscaping and regularized by the grid.
The earliest housing dates from 100 years ago, and was designed in the stick style or Eastlake style. (The stick style is "... characterized by the use of exposed framing overlaid on clapboard...to suggest structural supports." The Eastlake style is similar to stick style, "... except for its distinctive three-dimensional scrollwork and gingerbread.") The presence of these or other styles of the period serves to emphasize the uniqueness of this neighborhood, possessing as it does works from a since-lost time of American domestic architectural excellence. These earliest structures often have their out-buildings and water-towers intact, thus suggesting that these were the main residences of orchard or small-farming operations. Many of these original structures are located along Twenty-first street, implying an earlier settlement of this street.
